The later you fly, the more likely you'll be late

An evening flight is three times as likely to arrive as a 6 a.m. flight. Look up your own route below. And when the airline says "your plane came in late," that delay usually started as the airline's own problem earlier in the day.

Show the numbers

How this was measured

The US Department of Transportation requires larger airlines to report every domestic flight: when it was scheduled, when it actually left and arrived, and, for every flight that arrived 15 or more minutes late, how many minutes to blame on each of five causes. This page uses every reported flight from .

The five causes, in plain words

  • The airline's own: crew, maintenance, cleaning, bags, fueling.
  • Handed down: the plane arrived late from its previous flight.
  • The system: air traffic control, congestion, airport operations, and everyday weather that slows traffic. Most weather delays land here.
  • Severe weather: weather bad enough to stop flights.
  • Security: under 1% of delay minutes; counted with the system in the charts.

Following delays back

Every flight record names the plane by its tail number, so a plane's flights can be lined up in order. When a flight's delay was handed down, we pass those minutes back to the causes of that plane's previous flight, in the same proportions, and keep going up the chain. If the previous flight was only a few minutes late (too little for a cause to be recorded) but left late, we keep following it back. A previous flight counts only if it landed at the airport this flight leaves from, within the past day, no more than 2 hours before this flight was due to leave.

This re-sorts what the airlines reported. It isn't an independent judgment of fault, and it only moves minutes the airline itself labeled as handed down.

Why some delays can't be followed back

    What this doesn't show

    • Only domestic flights by the airlines that must report, plus the regional airlines that fly for them.
    • Hour of day overlaps with other things: evening flights are more often at busy hubs and in thunderstorm season. These are the odds a traveler faces, not proof the hour itself causes delay.
    • "Typical delay" is the among late arrivals.
